evidence.summary: ACP is a JSON-RPC-over-stdio wire protocol standardizing communication between code editors/clients and coding agents (Rust schema crate + Kotlin/Java/Python/TypeScript/Rust SDKs). It defines session lifecycle (session/new, session/load, session/update streaming notifications), a permission-request flow, and an authentication handshake, but is protocol-level only: it carries no login of its own and no worker/dispatch/orchestration layer. Native fit is entirely inherited from whichever agent process implements the ACP server side (Claude Code via Zed's adapter, Codex CLI via an adapter, Gemini CLI, etc.).
evidence.interface: Stdio JSON-RPC 2.0 wire protocol between a Client (editor/IDE) and an Agent subprocess. Methods include initialize (capability/version negotiation), authenticate, session/new, session/load, session/prompt, session/update (server->client streaming notifications), session/cancel, and session/request_permission. Official SDKs: Rust (agent-client-protocol / agent-client-protocol-schema crates), TypeScript (@agentclientprotocol/sdk), Python (python-sdk), Kotlin (acp-kotlin), Java (java-sdk). JSON Schema artifacts published per release under schema/v1 and schema/v2.
evidence.auth_model: Two authentication method types per the docs: default type 'agent', where 'the Agent handles authentication itself' (i.e., whatever the wrapped CLI already does — for Claude Code or Codex this would be their existing native/API-key login, invoked inside the agent subprocess), and 'terminal', where the Client 'Launches a separate interactive process using the same configured Agent program' with supplied args/env so the user completes an interactive login (e.g. a `codex login` or `claude login`-style flow) and the agent's exit status signals success/failure. The initialize handshake exposes an authMethods array (id/name/description) the client can call via the `authenticate` method. ACP itself defines no credential store or key of its own.
evidence.isolation_model: Session-scoped, not process-sandboxed by the protocol itself. session/new and session/load require an absolute `cwd` that 'MUST be used for the session regardless of where the Agent subprocess was spawned' and 'MUST remain the base for relative-path resolution.' Each session keeps 'its own context, conversation history, and state, allowing multiple independent interactions with the same Agent.' Actual OS-level sandboxing/isolation is left to the wrapped agent implementation (e.g. Claude Code's own worktree/sandbox behavior, or Codex's), not to ACP.
evidence.worker_features: No native multi-worker or dispatch/orchestration concept in the protocol; it is a single Client<->single Agent session channel. Concurrency across worktrees/sandboxes would have to be built by running multiple ACP client<->agent pairs externally (one per worktree), which the protocol permits but does not provide tooling for. MCP server connections can be attached per-session ('Clients MAY include connection details for MCP servers that the Agent should connect to'; stdio transport mandatory, HTTP/SSE optional), giving custom-tool extensibility.
evidence.structured_events: session/update is a streaming notification carrying a SessionUpdate union with concrete variants observed in the schema docs: agent_message_chunk (streamed LLM content), tool_call, tool_call_update (tool invocation lifecycle), plan (agent's execution strategy), available_commands_update, config_option_update, current_mode_update. Sensitive operations trigger session/request_permission, giving the client a RequestPermissionRequest with tool-call detail and permission options, answered with a RequestPermissionOutcome. session/load requires the Agent to 'replay the entire conversation to the Client' for resumption, distinct from a plain resume (no replay before responding) — this is the resumable-session mechanism the shortlist reasons point to.
evidence.tests_and_ci: No dedicated top-level `tests/` directory in the repo root listing (confirms the judges' has_tests_dir=false note), but .github/workflows/ci.yml runs a real CI pipeline on every push/PR to main: cargo check at MSRV, npm-based formatting/typo checks, cargo clippy across multiple feature combinations, cargo build --all-targets --all-features, docs.rs build check, `cargo test --all-features` (a real, executed-in-CI Rust test suite, just not under a top-level tests/ folder), a generated-files-up-to-date check, plus a separate feature-powerset job (4-way partitioned matrix) gated on detected Rust changes. findings.claim: overlap_with_incumbents: "No incumbent in the named list is an agent-driving stdio JSON-RPC protocol; the modelcontextprotocol SDKs entry is the closest by name but is the opposite direction."
findings.problem: False as written, and refutable without network access. The incumbent openai/codex ships its own agent-driving JSON-RPC-over-stdio protocol, `codex app-server` (default `--listen stdio://`, plus generate-json-schema and generate-ts bindings). I generated its schema bundle locally: the v2 protocol defines 102 ClientRequest methods, 82 ServerNotification types and 10 ServerRequest types, and maps one-to-one onto every ACP surface the packet names as the differentiator - initialize<->initialize, thread/start<->session/new, thread/resume + thread/items/list<->session/load (replay), turn/start<->session/prompt, turn/interrupt<->session/cancel, item/permissions/requestApproval + item/commandExecution/requestApproval + item/fileChange/requestApproval<->session/request_permission, item/started|item/completed|item/agentMessage/delta|turn/plan/updated<->session/update variants, account/login/start<->authenticate, mcpServer/tool/call<->per-session MCP attachment. The only surviving ACP differentiator is one wire format across vendors, not a capability the incumbents lack - far narrower than the C5 reasoning two of three judges used to reach targeted_candidate.

CAO's isolation is tmux-session-level with a shared filesystem by default (agents "start in supervisor's current directory" unless a `working_directory` override points them elsewhere) — this is weaker than the project's worktree-per-writer contract (`isolation: worktree`, EnterWorktree/ExitWorktree) and does not by itself give deterministic per-worker filesystem ownership. Its genuine potential edge is cross-vendor orchestration in one run (driving a Claude Code process and a Codex process together under real native logins, not simulated via two separate CLI sessions), which the Claude-only Workflow tool cannot do natively — but this project already has a defined cross-family lane (`docs/codex-coop-lanes.md`, `/codex:review`) for that purpose, so CAO's value-add specifically is whether CAO's tmux+event-bus orchestration gives more (isolation, structured events, resumability) than the existing Codex-coop lanes for a bounded cross-family task.

CAO ships a git-worktree provisioning service: src/cli_agent_orchestrator/services/worktree_service.py, whose module docstring names exactly the gap the packet asserts CAO lacks ("they share the same git branch and working directory by default -- the exact 'merge conflicts, overwritten files, race conditions' gap issue #100 names. Worktree path and branch are derived deterministically from the server-generated terminal_id (WORKTREE_SUBDIR = ".cao/worktrees", BRANCH_PREFIX = "cao/"), i.e. structural per-worker ownership, not manual working_directory configuration. docs/api.md confirms the API surface: "Terminal creation accepts use_worktree (bool, default false, issue #100 Phase 1): provisions an isolated git worktree on its own branch instead of sharing working_directory as given ... At deletion, the worktree's working-tree contents are always discarded, but the branch is only deleted if it has no unmerged commits." The packet's whole isolation contrast with the project's worktree contract, and the risk derived from it, rest on evidence the packet did not read (it read only docs/tmux.md and docs/working-directory.md, neither of which covers use_worktree). evidence.summary: Vibe Kanban (BloopAI/vibe-kanban, Apache-2.0, Rust+TS) is a local kanban board that dispatches coding-agent CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, Amp, Cursor, OpenCode, Droid, CCR, Qwen Code) into per-task git worktrees, streams diffs to a review UI, and exposes an MCP server for workspace/session/prompt control. evidence.summary: Gemini CLI is an open-source, Apache-2.0 terminal AI agent from Google. It offers a headless/non-interactive `-p`/`--prompt` mode with JSON and streaming-JSONL structured event output, MCP-based tool extensibility, checkpointing/session resume, and a documented multi-tier sandbox model (Docker/Podman, macOS Seatbelt, optional gVisor). It authenticates natively via 'Login with Google' OAuth (free tier), a Gemini API key, or Vertex AI credentials, satisfying C1 with an existing Google login rather than a separate paid key by default. Active release cadence (stable weekly, v0.60.0 on 2026-09-15, nightly builds daily) and CI badges/integration-tests/test-utils package are present, satisfying C4. It is a targeted_candidate for a bounded head-to-head against `codex exec`, not yet adopted.
evidence.interface: CLI with headless/non-interactive mode: `gemini -p "<prompt>"` or piping input in a non-TTY context. Supports `--output-format json` (single JSON object with response text and usage/latency stats) and a streaming JSONL mode emitting typed events (`init`, `message`, `tool_use`, `tool_result`, `error`, `result`). Standardized exit codes: 0 success, 1 general/API error, 42 input validation failure, 53 turn-limit exceeded. Also has an Extensions API (custom slash-commands/bundles) and a `packages/sdk` package in the monorepo (programmatic use beyond the bare CLI, not independently verified here).
evidence.auth_model: Three authentication paths, per docs and README: (1) OAuth 'Login with Google' — opens a browser login prompt, 'requires no keys or environment variables and offers the most generous free tier' (README: 'Free tier: 60 requests/min and 1,000 requests/day with personal Google account'); (2) a Gemini API key from Google AI Studio, noted to have 'much lower limits on the unpaid tier compared to the OAuth method'; (3) Vertex AI, via Application Default Credentials (gcloud), a service-account JSON key, or a Google Cloud API key, requiring GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT and GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION to be set.
evidence.isolation_model: Documented multi-tier sandbox, selected via the GEMINI_SANDBOX environment variable: macOS Seatbelt process-level profiles (permissive-open default, permissive-proxied, restrictive-open, restrictive-proxied, strict-open, strict-proxied) restricting filesystem/network/syscalls; cross-platform Docker/Podman container sandboxing with process, filesystem and network isolation via controlled volume mounts; and an optional gVisor (runsc) user-space kernel layer described as the strongest isolation tier. This is a per-invocation sandbox configuration, not inherently a per-worktree isolation primitive — running it inside an owned worktree (as the shortlist's comparison proposes) would rely on the caller's own directory choice plus the sandbox's volume-mount scoping, not a CLI-native worktree concept.
evidence.worker_features: MCP (Model Context Protocol) client support for wiring custom tools/servers, configured via an `mcpServers` object naming server command/args; a CLI command lists configured MCP servers, connection status and available tools. An Extensions API lets users build and share custom commands/bundles. No evidence found in this pass of a native multi-agent/subagent dispatch or worker-pool primitive comparable to Claude Code's Agent/Workflow tools or Codex's custom agents — MCP tool-calling and extensions are the closest documented mechanisms.
evidence.structured_events: Streaming JSONL headless mode emits typed events per the official headless-mode docs: `init` (session metadata), `message` (user/assistant message chunks), `tool_use` (tool invocation with arguments), `tool_result` (tool execution output), `error` (non-fatal warnings), and `result` (final outcome with aggregated stats). Non-streaming JSON mode returns one object with response text plus token-usage/latency stats and optional error details.

evidence.summary: mini-swe-agent (SWE-agent org) is a pure-Python, MIT-licensed, ~100-line-core coding agent, installable via pip/uvx/pipx as a CLI (`mini`) and importable as a library (DefaultAgent/LitellmModel/LocalEnvironment). It has upstream tests (tests/ with pytest CI, pylint CI, Codecov badge) and an active release cadence (5 releases from 2026-06-18 to 2026-07-23, latest v2.4.6, repo pushed 2026-09-21 — 0 days before this evidence pull). It executes each agent action as an independent subprocess.run/docker-exec-style call (no persistent shell session) against a pluggable Environment (local/no-isolation, Docker, Podman, Singularity/Apptainer, experimental Linux-only Bubblewrap, or "contree"), giving it the strongest deterministic/no-hidden-global-state profile in the C3 sense of the harnesses judged in this slice. It supports fully headless operation via `--yolo` plus stdin-redirect detection, and writes a flat JSON trajectory (`last_mini_run.traj.json`) as its structured-event record; no MCP integration or explicit resumable-session API was found. Authentication is entirely LiteLLM-routed (provider API key or a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint such as vLLM) — it does not consume any native Claude Code/Codex/GitHub/Google login, which is a recorded C1 penalty, not an exclusion, and it also fits the project's existing local vLLM branch. Given the preregistered rule that judge agreement never promotes, and this repo's clear functional overlap with Claude Code's `-p` headless mode and Codex `exec`, the disposition here is targeted_candidate / keep_but_compare: worth an executed comparison (mini-swe-agent vs. a Claude Code `-p` run, or vs. Codex exec, on one bounded local fixture task against the shared local vLLM endpoint, scoring trajectory determinism/reproducibility and patch correctness/tokens-per-solved-task), not adoption.
